title: Green Sea Turtles Are Bouncing Back — But the Job Isn't Done
summary:
On a quiet beach after dark, a green sea turtle hauls herself out of the ocean and up the sand, leaving a trail of alternating flipper marks that look like tire tracks from a monster truck. She is looking for a place to lay her eggs. On Aldabra, a remote atoll 400 miles off the eastern coast of Africa, that sight is far more common than it was 50 years ago.

Green turtles were once hunted heavily for meat, leather, and eggs. At the end of the 19th century, as many as 12,000 green turtles were captured at Aldabra in a single year. By the 1960s, annual nests on the atoll had fallen to just 2,000 to 3,000.

A hunting ban in 1968 gave Aldabra's turtles a key safeguard. Researchers at the atoll's station — fewer than three dozen people live there — have now tracked nesting turtles for more than half a century. The wait was long because green turtles do not start breeding until they are 25 to 35 years old, so a generation born under protection needed decades to return. But return they did: in 2019, staff estimated more than 15,000 clutches of eggs across the atoll, a 173 percent increase since 1980. On Settlement Beach alone, researchers can find close to 100 turtles in one night at peak season.

The comeback is global. In October 2025, the International Union for Conservation of Nature moved green turtles from endangered to least concern. The IUCN estimated worldwide numbers have risen roughly 28 percent since the 1970s, and a separate 2025 assessment found 8 of their 11 regional populations at low risk.

Satellite tracking shows why one beach matters so much: turtles from Aldabra travel more than 1,500 miles, fanning out like the crooked spokes of a wheel to feed on seagrass as far away as Somalia, Mozambique, and the southern tip of Madagascar.

But the recovery is uneven. A small population in the south-central Pacific remains in serious trouble from bycatch, hunting, and climate change, and other populations in the East Pacific, southwest Pacific, and North Indian Oceans are vulnerable. Environmental economist Adam Pritchard calls it a conservation success story — and adds that the work is definitely not done.
why_it_matters: Aldabra's recovery shows that long-term protection can bring a hunted species back, but the uneven picture means conservation work still matters for the populations that remain at risk.

background_read: Green sea turtles are large sea animals that come ashore to lay eggs in sandy nests on beaches.
For a long time people hunted them for food and other products, which pushed their numbers down.
A hunting ban protects them, and researchers count nests to track whether the population is recovering.
Because turtles take many years to start breeding, a recovery can take decades to show up.
